The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Crimson snapper (Lutjanus erythropterus) was 25% [GSI = 25%], documented in field-caught mature females sampled during the spawning season at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This measurement was obtained at a relatively stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], which reflects typical conditions experienced on the continental shelf during the peak reproductive months. The index indicates that ovarian tissue constitutes about a quarter of the total body mass, a proportion that aligns with the energy-intensive spawning strategy common among lutjanids. This species exhibits a protracted spawning period, with females likely releasing multiple batches of pelagic eggs over several months.

Females of this species attain reproductive maturity at a fork length of 48.6 centimeters [Lp = 48.6 centimeters], a size that corresponds to approximately two to three years of age under average growth conditions in the wild. This length at puberty marks the threshold at which vitellogenesis begins and gonad development accelerates, enabling first participation in the annual spawning aggregations. The size at which females become capable of reproduction is an important demographic parameter, influencing the resilience of the population to fishing pressure. Juveniles and sub-adults grow rapidly during their early years, but the onset of maturity represents a notable shift in energy allocation from somatic growth to reproductive investment. Individuals smaller than this length have immature gonads and do not contribute to the annual reproductive output. The length at puberty for females is a key reference point for fisheries management, as it defines the minimum size at which the stock can sustain itself through successful recruitment.

Growth in the species ultimately plateaus at an asymptotic fork length of 81.6 centimeters [Li = 81.6 centimeters], which represents the maximum average size that a fully grown adult can reach under natural conditions. This ultimate fork length is a product of the species' growth trajectory, which follows a decelerating pattern typical of many long-lived tropical reef fishes. Individuals approach this size after many years of steady growth, but the rate of length increase slows considerably once sexual maturity has been achieved. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an individual of this length is approximately 4300 grams [Wwi = approximately 4300 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships established for closely related stock. This large body size confers several advantages, including higher fecundity, improved competitive ability on the reef, and reduced vulnerability to most predators. The combination of a substantial asymptotic size and a relatively slow growth rate underscores the importance of protecting older, larger individuals to maintain the reproductive capacity of the population.

At the earliest stage of life, the wet weight at birth for a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is estimated to be 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a minute mass derived from the diameter of the fertilised egg. This initial weight reflects the limited endogenous yolk reserves that the lecithotrophic larva must rely upon before the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolksac period is brief, lasting only a few days, during which the non-feeding larva undergoes rapid organogenesis and swim bladder inflation. The small birth weight imposes a tight time window for successful first prey capture once the yolk is fully resorbed; failure to transition to active feeding within this period leads to starvation and mortality. Mortality rates during the early larval phase are exceptionally high, a common bottleneck in the life history of marine fishes. The minute size of the newly emerged prolarva also renders it highly susceptible to a wide array of planktonic predators in the pelagic environment. This critical early stage sets the foundation for subsequent recruitment success.

Longevity records indicate that the maximum lifespan of Crimson snapper is approximately 32 years [am = approximately 32 years], though this figure must be interpreted with the understanding that the animals were maintained under thermal conditions averaging 28 °C [T = 28 °C] during the study period. The attainment of asymptotic size, combined with an extended adult phase, suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes survival and iteroparous reproduction over rapid turnover. Senescence in this species is likely gradual, with reproductive output potentially declining only in the very oldest individuals. The elevated temperature may slightly accelerate metabolic processes and influence the rate of aging, but the species appears well-adapted to the warm waters of its tropical habitat. Such extended longevity underscores the species' vulnerability to overexploitation, as recovery from population depletion can require many decades.
